body:
# Akṣobhya — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Akṣobhya, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Akṣobhya to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **अक्षोभ्य**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Akṣobhya**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: uk-SHOH-bhyuh — the kṣ is a single conjunct sound (k + retroflex ṣ); the bh is aspirated. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *akshobhya* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *akshobhya* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible.  A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

Now to the forms that provoked your letter. As for *akshobya*: it comes from the anglicized respelling — the name written the way English guesses it sounds, and it fails because rewrites attested consonant clusters to fit English spelling habits; every cluster simplified this way erases a letter the sources write

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. China received him early as Āchù and later rendered him "the Immovable" — a name he shares as a near-doublet with Acala, the blazing Fudō Myōō of Japan, whose wrathful immovability is the mirror image of his serene one.  Tibet made Mi bskyod pa central to the highest tantras and to the rites of death and purification, and the five-Buddha system that enthrones him traveled from the Indian universities to every Himalayan valley.

And it never stopped working. Akṣobhya's legacy is the mirror itself: the image of mind as a reflecting surface that needs only to stay still became one of the deep metaphors of East Asian Buddhism, from Huayan to Zen.  His earth-touching gesture — assigned to him among the five — is the most reproduced Buddha pose on earth, the seal of the historical awakening reassigned to the unshakable one.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Akṣobhya** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *akshobhya* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Akṣobhya** stands at [/sites/akshobhya/](/sites/akshobhya/).

The docket for this ruling: 1 false form ruled against, *akshobya* first on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Akṣobhya-tathāgatasya-vyūha Sūtra, Guhyasamāja Tantra, Conze.
